#1
L: Who, the injunction-of-scripture having-abandoned, sacrifice endowed-with-faith — of them the steadfastness, but, what, Kṛṣṇa? Sattva, or rajas, tamas?
I: Those who, disregarding the injunction of scripture, offer sacrifice endowed with faith — what is their footing, Kṛṣṇa? Is it sattva, or rajas, or tamas?
N: Arjuna opens the chapter with a question left over from the last: chapter 16 closed by making scripture (śāstra) the standard for action, and here Arjuna asks about people who ignore that standard yet still sacrifice with real fervor (śraddhayā anvitāḥ, 'endowed with faith' — śraddhayā+anvitāḥ, ā+a→ā). Niṣṭhā, 'steadfastness, footing, standing', asks what ground such people are really standing on. Sattvam āho rajas tamaḥ is not a compound: sattva, rajas and tamas are three separate alternatives (rajaḥ tamaḥ simply written together at their sandhi boundary, -aḥ+t-→-as t-), with āho, 'or', an interrogative disjunctive particle. This opens the chapter's governing question — is faith itself always good, or does its worth depend on which guṇa shapes it? — which Kṛṣṇa begins to answer immediately in verse 2. Sattva, rajas, tamas, the three guṇas, are kept untranslated throughout, per convention.
#2
L: Threefold comes-to-be the-faith of-embodied-beings, it, born-of-own-nature: sattva-natured, and rajas-natured, and-indeed tamas-natured — thus; hear it.
I: The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature: sattva-natured, rajas-natured, and tamas-natured. Hear now what these are.
N: Kṛṣṇa answers directly, with no speaker-line question of his own (the speaker line at the head of this verse is generated separately; see conventions.md). Svabhāvajā, 'born of one's own nature', makes the chapter's first and most important claim: faith is not simply chosen, it grows out of the disposition each person already has. Sāttvikī, rājasī, tāmasī are feminine forms agreeing with śraddhā; ca eva fuses to caiva (a+e→ai) and ca iti to ceti (a+i→e). This threefold division of faith itself, before any of its outward expressions, frames everything that follows through verse 22.
#3
L: Conformed-to-[one's-own]-nature of-everyone, faith comes-to-be, Bhārata; made-of-faith [is] this person: who has-whatever-faith, he indeed [is] that.
I: Each person's faith conforms to his own nature, Bhārata. A person is made of faith: whatever his faith is, that indeed is what he is.
N: Sattva-anurūpā is ambiguous and worth flagging: here sattva does not mean the guṇa named in verse 1, but (per Śaṅkara) the antaḥkaraṇa, one's inner constitution or disposition — the particular blend of the three guṇas peculiar to each person — so it is translated 'nature' rather than left as the untranslated guṇa-name. Yat-śraddhaḥ (yad+śraddha, -t+ś-→-c ch-) is a bahuvrīhi, 'he whose faith is such-and-such'; sa eva saḥ doubles the pronoun for emphasis, 'he is precisely that' — the poem's most compact statement that a person's character is his faith. The pronoun sa (not saḥ) is written without visarga before any consonant, a standing exception in Sanskrit orthography.
#4
L: The-sattva-natured sacrifice to-gods; to-yakṣas-and-rākṣasas, the-rajas-natured; and to-ghosts-and-hosts-of-spirits, other tamas-natured people sacrifice.
I: The sattva-natured worship the gods; the rajas-natured worship yakṣas and rākṣasas; and other, tamas-natured people worship ghosts and hosts of spirits.
N: Verse 2's threefold faith is now shown in its first outward form — the object of worship each type of person is drawn to. Yakṣa-rakṣāṃsi is a dvandva (pair-compound), 'yakṣas and rākṣasas', taking the neuter plural ending of its last member rakṣas; yakṣas and rākṣasas, like preta ('a departed spirit, a ghost') and bhūta-gaṇa ('a host of elemental spirits'), are kept as their proper Sanskrit class-names rather than translated, following the pipeline's practice for such mythological categories (cf. 10.23, 11.22). Anye, 'other', agrees with tāmasāḥ janāḥ, completing the triad of worshippers that matches verse 2's triad of faith.
#5
L: Terrible austerity-not-enjoined-by-scripture practice the-people who [do so], joined-with-hypocrisy-and-egotism, possessed-by-the-force-of-desire-and-passion,
I: Those people who practice terrible austerities not enjoined by scripture, joined with hypocrisy and egotism, driven by the force of desire and passion,
N: This verse opens a sentence that the main verb (viddhi, 'know') completes only in verse 6 — a relative-correlative spanning both verses (ye ... tān). A-śāstra-vihitam, 'not enjoined by scripture', recalls the very standard chapter 16 closed on (śāstraṃ pramāṇaṃ te, 16.24) and that verse 1's question already invoked; dambha, 'hypocrisy', was named repeatedly among the demonic traits of chapter 16 (16.4, 17-18). Tapaḥ here is the accusative object of tapyante ('they practice austerity'), not yet the topic named formally at verse 7.
#6
L: Tormenting the-aggregate-of-[bodily]-elements situated-in-the-body, mindless, and me too, dwelling-within-the-body — know them [to be] of-demonic-resolve.
I: Mindlessly they torment the mass of elements that make up the body, and me as well, dwelling within it — know them to be demonic in their resolve.
N: This is the chapter's one point where the received (vulgate) text, printed here, differs from the BORI critical edition: the vulgate reads karṣayantaḥ, 'tormenting, dragging down' (from √kṛṣ), where BORI reads karśayantaḥ, 'emaciating, wasting away' (from √kṛś) — a real vulgate/BORI variant, not a misprint. Bhūta-grāmam, 'the aggregate of [bodily] elements', names the physical body itself, contrasted with antar-śarīra-stham mām, 'me, dwelling within the body' (surface antaḥ- before the unvoiced ś-) — the same inner presence taught elsewhere as the kṣetrajña (ch. 13) or the self seated in the heart (15.15). Tān, 'those', picks up verse 5's ye, closing the two-verse sentence; āsura-niścayān, 'of demonic resolve', is Kṛṣṇa's verdict on such self-torturers, who harm not only their own bodies but, unknowingly, the god within them.
#7
L: Food too, indeed, of-everyone threefold comes-to-be, dear; sacrifice, austerity, and-likewise giving — of-these this distinction, hear.
I: Food too is dear to everyone, but of three different kinds; so are sacrifice, austerity, and giving. Hear now how they differ.
N: This verse names the chapter's remaining four topics — āhāra ('food', vv. 8-10), yajña ('sacrifice', vv. 11-13), tapas ('austerity', vv. 14-19) and dāna ('giving', vv. 20-22) — each to be classified, like faith and worship before them, into its sattva-, rajas- and tamas-natured forms. Priyaḥ, 'dear, agreeable', signals that what a person finds appetizing or satisfying is itself diagnostic of guṇa, just as what they worship was in verse 4.
#8
L: Lifespan-vitality-strength-health-happiness-and-satisfaction-increasing; savory, unctuous, firm, heart-pleasing — [such] foods [are] dear-to-the-sattva-natured.
I: Foods that increase lifespan, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and satisfaction; savory, rich, substantial, and pleasing to the heart — such foods are dear to the sattva-natured.
N: This opens the food-triad (vv. 8-10). The long opening compound āyuḥ-sattva-bala-ārogya-sukha-prīti-vivardhanāḥ packs six benefits into one word; note that sattva here means 'vitality, vigor' — a secondary sense of the word distinct from its use as one of the three guṇas named throughout this chapter (compare the different, generic sense of sattva already flagged at verse 3). Rasyāḥ, snigdhāḥ, sthirāḥ, hṛdyāḥ describe food by taste and texture rather than nutritional effect, closing with sāttvika-priyāḥ, 'dear to the sattva-natured', the formula this triad repeats for each guṇa (cf. verses 9-10).
#9
L: Pungent-sour-salty-excessively-hot-sharp-dry-burning — [such] foods [are] favored-of-the-rajas-natured, causing-pain-grief-and-disease.
I: Foods that are pungent, sour, salty, very hot, acrid, dry, and burning — these are favored by the rajas-natured, and they bring on pain, grief, and disease.
N: The rajas-natured diet, named through a seven-member compound whose internal sandhi is worth tracing: kaṭu+amla→kaṭvamla (u+a→va, yaṇ), lavaṇa+ati→lavaṇāti (a+a→ā), ati+uṣṇa→atyuṣṇa (i+u→yu, yaṇ). Duḥkha-śoka-āmaya-pradāḥ, 'causing pain, grief and disease', states the cost of such food as bluntly as verse 8 stated sattva's food's benefits.
#10
L: Stale, flat, putrid, and kept-overnight, and also — leftover and impure — food [is] dear-to-the-tamas-natured.
I: Food that is stale, flat, putrid, and kept overnight, and also food that is leftover and unclean — such food is dear to the tamas-natured.
N: Closes the food-triad. Yāta-yāmam, literally 'past its watch', is the standard idiom for stale food; gata-rasam, 'having lost its flavor'; ucchiṣṭam, 'a remnant of a meal', and amedhyam, 'unfit for sacrifice, impure', name food considered ritually unclean as well as physically unappetizing. Bhojana, 'food', here simply varies āhāra of verses 8-9.
#11
L: The-sacrifice by-those-not-desiring-the-fruit, prescribed-by-rule, which is offered, — '[it]-is-indeed-to-be-offered' — thus the-mind having-fixed — that [is] sattva-natured.
I: A sacrifice offered by those without desire for its fruit, performed as the rule prescribes, with the mind fixed only on 'this must be offered' — that is sattva-natured.
N: Opens the sacrifice-triad (vv. 11-13). Aphala-ākāṅkṣibhiḥ, 'by those not desiring the fruit' (a+ā→ā within the compound), echoes the poem's standing teaching on action without regard for its results (cf. 2.47); vidhi-dṛṣṭaḥ, 'as prescribed by rule', ties proper performance to scripture, as verse 1 raised and 16.24 already taught. Yaṣṭavyam eva iti manaḥ samādhāya, 'having fixed the mind on "it is simply to be offered"', names duty performed for its own sake as the mark of sattva. Note the visarga elided (with hiatus retained) before a following vowel in य/इज्यते — an epic-verse option already flagged at 16.1.
#12
L: But, aiming-at the fruit, and-indeed also for-the-sake-of-ostentation, which is offered, best-of-the-Bharatas — that sacrifice know [to be] rajas-natured.
I: But the sacrifice offered with an eye on its reward, and also for the sake of show, best of the Bharatas — know that sacrifice to be rajas-natured.
N: Abhisaṃdhāya phalam, 'having aimed at the fruit', directly opposes verse 11's aphala-ākāṅkṣibhiḥ; dambha-artham, 'for the sake of ostentation', names the vice condemned repeatedly in chapter 16 (16.4, 17-18) now shown at work in ritual itself.
#13
L: Lacking-rule, without-the-giving-of-food, lacking-mantras, without-the-priestly-fee, devoid-of-faith — that sacrifice they call tamas-natured.
I: A sacrifice that ignores the proper procedure, gives out no food, lacks the mantras, offers no fee to the priests, and is without faith — that they call tamas-natured.
N: Closes the sacrifice-triad. A-sṛṣṭa-annam, 'without the giving-out of food' (the customary distribution of food or alms at a sacrifice, here omitted), and a-dakṣiṇam, 'without the priestly fee' (dakṣiṇā, the payment due the officiating priests), name specific lapses in proper form; śraddhā-virahitam, 'devoid of faith', closes the list by naming the very quality the chapter opened by asking about (verse 1) — a sacrifice performed with fervor but without proper form and without faith is, in the end, tamas-natured.
#14
L: Reverence-for-gods-brahmins-teachers-and-the-wise, purity, [and] uprightness; celibacy and non-violence — [this] austerity [is] called bodily.
I: Reverence for gods, brahmins, teachers, and the wise; purity, uprightness, celibacy, and non-violence — this is called austerity of the body.
N: Opens the austerity-section (vv. 14-19), first classified by where the effort is made — bodily (śārīra, this verse), verbal (vāṅmaya, v. 15), mental (mānasa, v. 16) — before being classified again by guṇa at verses 17-19. Dvija, 'twice-born', means a brahmin (as at 1.7's dvijottama); brahmacarya, literally 'conduct proper to Vedic study', is translated here as 'celibacy', the ascetic practice of sexual restraint it denotes, distinct from brahman itself, which stays untranslated. Tapa ucyate shows a visarga fully elided before the following vowel, with the hiatus kept rather than the vowels fusing — an accepted option in epic verse, already flagged at 16.1's svādhyāyas tapa ārjavam.
#15
L: Speech not-causing-distress, truthful, and pleasant-and-beneficial, and-indeed the-regular-practice-of-[Vedic]-recitation — [this] austerity [is] called verbal.
I: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, together with the regular recitation of one's own scriptures — this is called austerity of speech.
N: The second of the three bodily/verbal/mental divisions. Svādhyāya, 'the recitation of one's own [portion of the] Veda', is the daily discipline already named at 16.1; vāṅ-mayam, 'made of speech' (vāc+maya, with c assimilating to ṅ before m), names the whole category. As at verse 14, tapa ucyate again shows the visarga-elision-with-hiatus pattern.
#16
L: Serenity of-mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, and purity-of-[one's-own]-nature — this austerity [is] called mental.
I: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-mastery, and purity of one's inner disposition — this is called austerity of the mind.
N: Closes the threefold division of austerity by location. Manaḥ prasādaḥ, 'serenity of mind', is written as two separate words rather than a compound but functions as a single idea; bhāva-saṃśuddhiḥ, 'purity of one's inner nature/disposition', closes the list — note bhāva here, like sattva at verse 3, names a person's general inner state rather than any single guṇa. With the threefold classification by location now complete, verses 17-19 classify this same threefold austerity again, this time by guṇa.
#17
L: With-supreme-faith practiced, that threefold austerity, by-men without-desire-for-the-fruit, disciplined — [this] they call sattva-natured.
I: That threefold austerity, practiced with the highest faith by men who are free from desire for its fruit and disciplined in themselves — this they call sattva-natured.
N: Tat trividham, 'that threefold [austerity]', reaches back to the śārīra/vāṅmaya/mānasa triad of verses 14-16, now reclassified — like sacrifice before it (vv. 11-13) — into its sattva-, rajas- and tamas-natured forms. Aphala-ākāṅkṣibhiḥ yuktaiḥ, 'by men without desire for the fruit, disciplined', echoes verse 11's identical phrase for sacrifice; śraddhayā parayā, 'with supreme faith', returns the chapter explicitly to its opening theme.
#18
L: For-the-sake-of-honor-respect-and-reverence, and-indeed also with-hypocrisy, austerity which is performed — that here [is] declared rajas-natured, unsteady, unstable.
I: Austerity performed for the sake of honor, respect, and reverence, and out of hypocrisy — that is declared here to be rajas-natured, unsteady and impermanent.
N: Satkāra-māna-pūjā-artham, 'for the sake of honor, respect and reverence [from others]', names the desire for outward recognition, paired with dambhena, 'with hypocrisy' — the same vice named at verse 12 for sacrifice. Calam a-dhruvam, 'unsteady, unstable', judges the fruit of such austerity as fleeting, unlike sattva's lasting result.
#19
L: Which austerity, out-of-deluded-obstinacy, with-the-affliction-of-oneself, is performed, or for-the-sake-of-the-destruction-of-another — that [is] declared tamas-natured.
I: Austerity performed out of deluded stubbornness, through self-torment, or in order to destroy another — that is declared to be tamas-natured.
N: Closes the austerity-triad. Mūḍha-grāheṇa, 'out of deluded obstinacy' (grāha, 'a grasp, a fixed and mistaken conviction'), recalls the self-torturing ascetics condemned already at verses 5-6; parasya utsādana-artham, 'for the sake of destroying another', names austerity turned to malice or black magic — the darkest of the three.
#20
L: '[It]-is-to-be-given' — thus, which gift is given to-one-who-cannot-repay, in-the-[right]-place and-[right]-time and to-a-worthy-recipient — that gift [is] held sattva-natured.
I: A gift given because 'it is simply right to give', to someone who can make no return, at the proper place and time and to a worthy recipient — that gift is held to be sattva-natured.
N: Opens the giving-triad (vv. 20-22), the last of the four topics named in verse 7. An-upakāriṇe, 'to one who cannot repay', rules out gift-giving as disguised exchange; deśe kāle ca pātre ca, 'in the [right] place and time and to a worthy recipient', names the three traditional conditions of a proper gift. Dātavyam iti, 'because it is simply to be given', echoes verse 11's yaṣṭavyam eva iti — duty performed because it is right, the recurring mark of sattva throughout this chapter.
#21
L: But which, for-the-sake-of-a-return-favor, or again aiming-at [future] reward, is given, and given-reluctantly — that gift [is] held rajas-natured.
I: But a gift given in hope of some favor in return, or again with an eye on the reward to come, and given grudgingly — that gift is held to be rajas-natured.
N: Prati-upakāra-artham, 'for the sake of a return favor', directly negates verse 20's an-upakāriṇe; pari-kliṣṭam, 'given with reluctance, grudgingly', marks the giver's inner state as much as the outer act.
#22
L: At-a-wrong-place-and-time which gift, to-unworthy-recipients, is given, without-proper-respect and with-contempt — that [is] declared tamas-natured.
I: A gift given at the wrong place and time, to unworthy recipients, without respect and with contempt — that is declared to be tamas-natured.
N: Closes the giving-triad, and with it the whole enumerative half of the chapter (faith, worship, food, sacrifice, austerity, giving), by negating each term of verse 20 in turn: a-deśa-kāle against deśe kāle (the single privative a- here negating the whole pair, not deśa alone), a-pātrebhyaḥ against pātre, a-sat-kṛtam avajñātam, 'given without respect and with contempt', against the implicit honor of a proper gift. Verse 23 turns to the chapter's final and most demanding topic: the threefold name of brahman.
#23
L: 'Oṃ', 'Tat', 'Sat' — thus, the-designation of-brahman threefold [is] held; by-that were-brahmins, and-the-Vedas, and-sacrifices ordained, of-old.
I: 'Oṃ', 'Tat', 'Sat' — this is remembered as the threefold designation of brahman. By it, in ancient times, brahmins, the Vedas, and sacrifices were established.
N: This opens the chapter's closing section (vv. 23-28) and names its whole subject in one breath: all four words of the verse's first line are written as a single fused token (oṃ+tat+sat+iti, the last junction -t+i-→-d i-). Brahman, which cannot itself be spoken, is traditionally held to have this threefold name (nirdeśa, 'designation, pointing-out'): oṃ, the sacred syllable uttered at the start of Vedic recitation and rites; tat, 'That', the pronoun by which the Upaniṣads point to brahman beyond all qualities (as in tat tvam asi); and sat, 'Being, the Real', brahman under the aspect of pure existence. Each of the three is then treated in turn — oṃ in verse 24, tat in verse 25, sat in verses 26-27. Brāhmaṇāḥ ... vihitāḥ purā, '[brahmins, Vedas and sacrifices] were established of old', states that the whole Vedic order draws its authority from this threefold name of brahman. Brahman stays untranslated per convention; oṃ, tat and sat, being the very subject of this passage, are likewise left untranslated here as its three names — unlike sat/asat from verse 26 on, where the same word is used in its ordinary sense and is translated (see the note to verse 26).
#24
L: Therefore, 'Oṃ' having-uttered, the-rites-of-sacrifice-giving-and-austerity, prescribed-by-rule, proceed constantly, of-those-who-expound-brahman.
I: So, with 'Oṃ' uttered first, the rites of sacrifice, giving, and austerity, as scripture prescribes, are constantly carried out among those who expound brahman.
N: Treats oṃ, the first of the three names just given. Brahma-vādinām, 'of those who expound/uphold brahman', names followers of Vedic tradition, whose rites are still customarily prefaced with the utterance of oṃ; tasmāt, 'therefore', ties this directly back to verse 23's naming of oṃ as brahman's first designation. Brahman again kept untranslated; oṃ likewise, as the subject just named.
#25
L: 'Tat' — thus, not-aiming-at the fruit, the-rites-of-sacrifice-and-austerity, and-the-rites-of-giving, various, are-performed by-those-desiring-liberation.
I: Uttering 'Tat', and without an eye on the fruit, those who desire liberation perform the various rites of sacrifice, austerity, and giving.
N: Treats tat, the second name. Tat iti anabhisaṃdhāya phalam, 'thinking "Tat", without aiming at the fruit', means performing the rite while inwardly identifying the act with brahman itself, so that its fruit is renounced — the same teaching on desireless action given throughout chapters 2-3 and again at 4.24's brahma-arpaṇaṃ brahma haviḥ. Mokṣa-kāṅkṣibhiḥ, 'by those desiring liberation', names the aim of such renunciation directly.
#26
L: In-the-sense-of-being and in-the-sense-of-goodness — thus this [word] 'sat' is-used; and, likewise, in-a-praiseworthy action, the-word-'sat' is-applied, son-of-Pṛthā.
I: In the sense of reality and in the sense of excellence — that is how the word 'sat' is used; and it is applied, Pārtha, to a praiseworthy action as well.
N: Opens the closing treatment of sat, the third name (vv. 26-27), by distinguishing its two basic senses: sad-bhāve, 'in the sense of being, of existing' (its plain ontological use), and sādhu-bhāve, 'in the sense of goodness, of excellence' (its evaluative use) — and further, of a praśaste karmaṇi, 'a praiseworthy action'. From this point on, unlike the formula oṃ tat sat of verses 23-24 (kept untranslated there as brahman's own name), sat names an ordinary word under analysis and is accordingly translated, here and in verses 27-28, as 'being/reality' or 'good' according to context, per the pipeline's settled practice for this chapter. Sandhi: sad-bhāve is sat+bhāve (-t+bh-→-d bh-); sac-chabdaḥ is sat+śabdaḥ (-t+ś-→-c ch-), the same assimilation already seen at 16.24's tasmāc-chāstram.
#27
L: In-sacrifice, in-austerity, and in-giving, steadfastness 'sat' is-also-called; and-indeed action directed-to-that-[same]-end is-termed 'sat' precisely.
I: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and giving is also called 'sat'; and any action directed to that end is likewise termed 'sat'.
N: Closes the sat-section. Sthitiḥ, 'steadfastness, constancy' — perseverance in the very practices classified by guṇa in verses 11-22 — is itself called sat; and tad-arthīyam karma, 'action directed to that [same] end' (i.e. done for the sake of, or in connection with, the sacrifice, austerity and giving just named in this same verse's first line — not a fresh reference to verse 25's mokṣa), is likewise so termed. The section ties the abstract oṃ-tat-sat formula of verses 23-24 back to the concrete triads of sacrifice, austerity and giving that filled most of the chapter.
#28
L: Without-faith [what is] offered, given, austerity practiced, and done — that is-called 'asat', son-of-Pṛthā; and that [is] not, hereafter, nor indeed here.
I: Whatever is offered, given, or done, or whatever austerity is practiced without faith — that is called 'asat', Pārtha; it is nothing, neither in the world to come nor in this one.
N: The chapter's close, naming asat, the negative counterpart of sat: whatever act — hutam, dattam, tapaḥ taptam, kṛtam, 'offered, given, austerity practiced, done' — is performed a-śraddhayā, 'without faith', is asat, worthless; and tat na ... pretya no iha, 'that is nothing, neither hereafter nor here' (no read as na+u, an emphatic 'nor indeed', a+u→o, guṇa sandhi). The verse closes the ring begun at the chapter's very first line (verse 1's yajante śraddhayā anvitāḥ), confirming that śraddhā, faith, is the one condition running beneath every triad the chapter has drawn — food, sacrifice, austerity, giving, and now even the very name of brahman.
